style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare Greek transliterations in amp with Strong's carried in notes; em-dashes used sparingly; transliterations ASCII-normalized relative to the lexicon's spellings.
chapterNote: Two arguments, one nerve. First, partiality: the assembly that seats the gold-ringed man up front and stands the poor man by the footstool has appointed itself a court of corrupt judges, forgotten that God chose the world's poor to be rich in faith, and broken the royal law -- love your neighbor as yourself -- which does not shatter into keepable pieces, for the Lawgiver behind 'do not commit adultery' is the same voice behind 'do not murder,' and stumbling at one point makes a man answerable to the whole. Speak and act as those judged by the law of liberty, for judgment is merciless to the man who showed none, and mercy triumphs over judgment. Second, the letter's famous engine-room: faith without works. The claimed faith that watches a brother go hungry and offers him a blessing instead of bread is dead in itself; the demons hold better theology and at least shudder. Abraham's offering of Isaac and Rahab's sheltering of the spies show what James means by justified by works -- not wages replacing trust, but living faith proved alive by what it does. A body without breath is a corpse, and faith without works is exactly that.

1.text: My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, together with favoritism toward persons.
1.amp: My brethren [adelphos], have not the faith [pistis] of our Lord [kurios] Jesus [Iesous] Christ [Christos], the Lord of glory [doxa], with respect of persons [prosopolempsia -- receiving the face].
1.notes: prosopolempsia (G4382) is literally 'receiving the face': judging by what the face and its trappings show. Set against the doxa (G1391), the glory of Christ, every earthly glitter that partiality bows to is exposed as costume jewelry.

2.text: For suppose a man comes into your assembly wearing a gold ring and shining clothes, and a poor man comes in too, in filthy rags,
2.amp: For if there come [eiserchomai] unto your assembly ['synagogue', sunagoge, the KJV margin] a man [aner] with a gold ring [chrusodaktulios -- gold-fingered], in goodly [lampros -- bright, shining] apparel [esthes], and there come in also a poor man [ptochos] in vile [rhuparos -- filthy] raiment [esthes];
2.notes: The assembly is still called a sunagoge (G4864), a mark of how early and how Jewish this letter is. chrusodaktulios (G5554), gold-fingered: rings were rank made visible. rhuparos (G4508) is the same filth-root as 1:21 -- the poor man wears what the church was told to strip off in another sense.

3.text: and you look admiringly at the one in the shining clothes and say, 'You, sir, sit here in this good seat,' while to the poor man you say, 'You can stand over there, or sit down here below my footstool.'
3.amp: And you have respect [epiblepo -- look upon with regard] to him that wears the gay [lampros] clothing [esthes], and say [epo] unto him, 'Sit [kathemai] thou here in a good place [kalos]'; and say to the poor [ptochos], 'Stand [histemi] thou there,' or 'sit here under [hupo] my footstool [hupopodion]:'
3.notes: epiblepo (G1914) is the attentive gaze -- elsewhere used of God regarding the lowly (cf. Luke 1:48), here misspent on tailoring. The seating chart is the theology: kathemai in honor, histemi against the wall, or the floor by the hupopodion (G5286).

4.text: Have you not divided yourselves into ranks right there, and set yourselves up as judges whose reasonings are evil?
4.amp: Are you not then partial [diakrino -- divided, making distinctions] in yourselves, and are become [ginomai] judges [krites] of evil [poneros] thoughts [dialogismos -- reasonings]?
4.notes: diakrino (G1252), the doubting-word of 1:6, now social: the divided man becomes a dividing church. They have set up a courtroom in the aisle, and the bench is staffed by poneros dialogismos (G4190, G1261) -- calculations of advantage dressed as ushering.

5.text: Listen, my beloved brothers: has God not chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom He promised to those who love Him?
5.amp: Hearken [akouo], my beloved [agapetos] brethren [adelphos], Has not God [theos] chosen [eklegomai -- elected, selected out] the poor [ptochos] of this world [kosmos] rich [plousios] in faith [pistis], and heirs [kleronomos] of the kingdom [basileia] which He has promised [epangello] to them that love [agapao] Him?
5.notes: eklegomai (G1586) is election-language: God's deliberate choice runs exactly opposite the church's seating chart (cf. 1 Corinthians 1:26-28). The ptochos (G4434) stands in the assembly as a kleronomos (G2818), an heir of the basileia -- royalty in work clothes.

6.text: But you have dishonored the poor man. Is it not the rich who oppress you, and drag you personally into court?
6.amp: But you have despised [atimazo -- dishonored, treated shamefully] the poor [ptochos]. Do not rich men [plousios] oppress [katadunasteuo -- exercise power down upon] you, and draw [helko -- drag] you before the judgment seats [kriterion]?
6.notes: atimazo (G818): the church stripped honor from the one man God had crowned. The irony is economic as well as spiritual -- katadunasteuo (G2616) is the boot of the powerful, and helko (G1670) the drag to the kriterion; they were flattering the very class that was suing them.

7.text: Is it not they who blaspheme the noble name by which you were called?
7.amp: Do not they blaspheme [blasphemeo -- revile, slander] that worthy [kalos -- beautiful, noble] name [onoma] by the which you are called [epikaleomai -- the name invoked over you]?
7.notes: The kalos onoma (G2570, G3686) is Christ's, epikaleomai (G1941) -- spoken over them, likely at baptism, the way a bride takes a name. Favoring the class that blasphemeo (G987) that name is courting the household's enemies at the household table.

8.text: If you truly fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself,' you do well;
8.amp: If you fulfil [teleo] the royal [basilikos -- kingly] law [nomos] according to [kata] the scripture [graphe], 'Thou shalt love [agapao] thy neighbour [plesion] as thyself,' you do [poieo] well [kalos]:
8.notes: basilikos (G937): the law is royal because the King gave it and the kingdom of verse 5 runs on it (cf. Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39). Loving the plesion (G4139) as yourself leaves no clause under which the poor man stands by the wall.

9.text: but if you show partiality to faces, you are working sin, and the law itself convicts you as transgressors.
9.amp: But if you have respect to persons [prosopolempteo -- receive the face], you commit [ergazomai -- work] sin [hamartia], and are convinced [elencho -- convicted, exposed] of the law [nomos] as transgressors [parabates -- those who step across the line].
9.notes: ergazomai (G2038): partiality is not a lapse of taste but worked hamartia (G266), labor in sin's employ. elencho (G1651) is courtroom conviction -- the same law they thought they were keeping reads the charge, and parabates (G3848) is the verdict.

10.text: For whoever keeps the whole law and yet stumbles at a single point has become guilty of all of it.
10.amp: For whosoever shall keep [tereo] the whole [holos] law [nomos], and yet offend [ptaio -- stumble] in one [heis] point, he is become [ginomai] guilty [enochos -- liable, answerable] of all [pas].
10.notes: The law is not a stack of separable statutes but one seamless will of one Lawgiver: ptaio (G4417), one stumble, and the man is enochos (G1777), answerable to the whole. The point is not that all sins are equal but that lawbreaking cannot be offset by law-keeping elsewhere.

11.text: For the One who said, 'You shall not commit adultery,' said also, 'You shall not murder.' Now if you never commit adultery and yet you murder, you stand a transgressor of the law.
11.amp: For He that said [epo], 'Do not commit adultery [moicheuo],' said also, 'Do not kill [phoneuo].' Now if you commit no adultery, yet if you kill, you are become [ginomai] a transgressor [parabates] of the law [nomos].
11.notes: The argument of verse 10 grounded in the Speaker: both commands come from one mouth (cf. Exodus 20:13-14), so breaking either defies the same Voice. James picks phoneuo (G5407) deliberately -- dishonoring the poor is murder's seed-form, as his Lord taught (cf. Matthew 5:21-22).

12.text: So speak, and so act, as men who will be judged by the law of liberty.
12.amp: So speak ye [laleo], and so do [poieo], as they that shall be [mello] judged [krino] by [dia] the law [nomos] of liberty [eleutheria].
12.notes: The nomos eleutheria (G3551, G1657) returns from 1:25: the freeing law is still the judging law. Speech and deed, laleo and poieo, the letter's constant pair -- both go into the record, and mello (G3195) makes the judgment certain, only its date unknown.

13.text: For the judgment is merciless to the one who showed no mercy; and mercy glories over judgment.
13.amp: For he shall have judgment [krisis] without mercy [anileos], that has shown [poieo] no mercy [eleos]; and mercy [eleos] rejoices ['glorieth', katakauchaomai, the KJV margin -- boasts over, triumphs over] against judgment [krisis].
13.notes: anileos (G448), mercy-less: the man who ran his assembly like a court of faces gets the courtroom he built (cf. Matthew 5:7; 18:32-35). But the last word is eleos (G1656) katakauchaomai (G2620) -- mercy standing over judgment like a victor, boasting; that is the gospel in five words.

14.text: What good is it, my brothers, if a man claims to have faith but has no works? Can that kind of faith save him?
14.amp: What does it profit [ophelos], my brethren [adelphos], though a man say [lego] he has faith [pistis], and have not works [ergon]? can that faith save [sozo] him?
14.notes: The verse turns on lego (G3004): a man says he has pistis -- the claim is all that is in evidence. The Greek article points at 'that faith', the claimed kind; James never doubts that real faith saves, only that this specimen is real. ophelos (G3786), the profit-question, is Ecclesiastes' audit applied to religion.

15.text: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking daily food,
15.amp: If a brother [adelphos] or sister [adelphe] be naked [gumnos -- bare, ill-clad], and destitute [leipo -- lacking] of daily [ephemeros] food [trophe],
15.notes: gumnos (G1131) here means threadbare rather than stripped, and ephemeros (G2184) is hand-to-mouth: needs measured in days, not seasons. Note adelphe (G79) -- the sister named alongside the brother; the test case lives inside the family.

16.text: and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace; be warmed and be filled,' and yet you give them nothing the body needs -- what good is that?
16.amp: And one of you say [epo] unto them, 'Depart [hupago] in peace [eirene], be ye warmed [thermaino] and filled [chortazo]'; notwithstanding you give [didomi] them not those things which are needful [epitedeios] to the body [soma]; what does it profit [ophelos]?
16.notes: The blessing is theologically flawless -- eirene, warmth, fullness -- and delivered with empty hands. epitedeios (G2006), the actually-needful things for the soma (G4983): faith that will not didomi (G1325), give, has volunteered its own diagnosis, and ophelos closes the frame from verse 14.

17.text: So also faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead.
17.amp: Even so faith [pistis], if it has not works [ergon], is dead [nekros], being alone ['by itself', kata heautou, the KJV margin].
17.notes: nekros (G3498) is the corpse-word, not 'weak' or 'sick': a claimed faith producing nothing is not ailing but deceased. The phrase kata heautou, by itself -- faith was never designed to exist unaccompanied, any more than fire without heat.

18.text: Yes, someone will say, 'You have faith; I have works.' Show me that faith of yours apart from any works, and by my works I will show you my faith.
18.amp: Yea, a man may say [ereo], 'Thou hast faith [pistis], and I have works [ergon]': show [deiknumi -- demonstrate, prove] me thy faith without [ek -- 'some copies read, by', the KJV margin] thy works, and I will show [deiknumi] thee my faith by [ek] my works.
18.notes: The challenge is evidentiary: deiknumi (G1166), demonstrate. Faith is invisible in itself; ergon (G2041) is the only exhibit it can enter. The imagined divider who treats faith and works as separable gifts gets both handed back welded together.

19.text: You believe that God is one. Good for you -- the demons believe that too, and they shudder.
19.amp: Thou believest [pisteuo] that there is one [heis] God [theos]; thou doest [poieo] well [kalos]: the devils [daimonion] also believe [pisteuo], and tremble [phrisso -- shudder, bristle].
19.notes: The creed cited is the Shema itself (cf. Deuteronomy 6:4), Israel's best sentence -- held, James notes, by every daimonion (G1140) in existence. phrisso (G5425) is hair-on-end shuddering: the demons' orthodoxy at least produces a physical response, which is more than the workless believer can show.

20.text: But are you willing to learn, you empty man, that faith apart from works is barren?
20.amp: But wilt thou [thelo] know [ginosko], O vain [kenos -- empty] man [anthropos], that faith [pistis] without [choris] works [ergon] is dead [nekros]?
20.notes: kenos (G2756): empty of the very works under discussion -- the man is his own counter-example. Some ancient copies read arge, 'idle, barren,' for the second 'dead'; either way the ledger shows nothing. Two witnesses are now called: Abraham and Rahab.

21.text: Was not Abraham our father shown righteous by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar?
21.amp: Was not Abraham [Abraam] our father [pater] justified [dikaioo -- declared righteous, vindicated] by [ek] works [ergon], when he had offered [anaphero -- offered up] Isaac [Isaak] his son [huios] upon the altar [thusiasterion]?
21.notes: The Aqedah (cf. Genesis 22): the offering came decades after Genesis 15:6 declared Abraham righteous by faith. dikaioo (G1344) here carries its demonstrative sense -- the altar vindicated, made visible, what God had long since reckoned. Paul and James cite the same man against opposite errors: legalism there, dead orthodoxy here.

22.text: You see that his faith was working together with his works, and by those works his faith was brought to completion.
22.amp: Seest thou [blepo] how faith [pistis] wrought with [sunergeo -- worked together with] his works [ergon], and by [ek] works was faith made perfect [teleioo -- completed, brought to its goal]?
22.notes: sunergeo (G4903): faith and works as co-laborers on one site, not rivals for one office. teleioo (G5048) is the completion-word of 1:4 -- on Moriah, faith reached its telos, full-grown and visible, the way fruit completes a tree.

23.text: And so the Scripture was fulfilled that says, 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness' -- and he was called the friend of God.
23.amp: And the scripture [graphe] was fulfilled [pleroo] which says [lego], 'Abraham [Abraam] believed [pisteuo] God [theos], and it was imputed [logizomai -- reckoned, credited] unto him for righteousness [dikaiosune]': and he was called [kaleo] the Friend [philos] of God.
23.notes: James quotes Genesis 15:6 -- the very verse Paul builds justification by faith upon (cf. Romans 4:3) -- and says Moriah pleroo (G4137), filled it full: the credit entry proved good when tested. philos theos (G5384): the title Scripture gives Abraham twice (cf. 2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8), friendship being what tested faith ripens into.

24.text: You see then that a man is shown righteous by works, and not by faith alone.
24.amp: You see [horao] then how that by [ek] works [ergon] a man [anthropos] is justified [dikaioo], and not by faith [pistis] only [monon].
24.notes: The sentence that has launched a thousand debates -- read in James's courtroom it is simple: the faith that justifies is never monon (G3440), never alone in the dock without its witness. Paul agrees from the other side: what avails is faith working through love (cf. Galatians 5:6).

25.text: In the same way, was not even Rahab the harlot shown righteous by works, when she took the messengers in and sent them out by another road?
25.amp: Likewise also was not Rahab [Rhaab] the harlot [porne] justified [dikaioo] by [ek] works [ergon], when she had received [hupodechomai -- welcomed under her roof] the messengers [angelos], and had sent them out [ekballo] another [heteros] way [hodos]?
25.notes: From the father of the faithful to a Canaanite porne (G4204): the doctrine holds at both ends of the social ladder, which is chapter 2's first argument returning. Rahab's pistis (cf. Joshua 2:9-11; Hebrews 11:31) went straight to work -- hupodechomai (G5264), rooftop flax, a scarlet cord -- and landed her in Messiah's own genealogy (cf. Matthew 1:5).

26.text: For just as a body with no breath in it is dead, so faith with no works is dead too.
26.amp: For as the body [soma] without [choris] the spirit ['breath', pneuma, the KJV margin] is dead [nekros], so faith [pistis] without works [ergon] is dead also.
26.notes: pneuma (G4151) here is the breath of life itself: a soma with no breath is not a lesser kind of body but a corpse awaiting burial. The analogy assigns the roles precisely -- works are not the soul of faith but its breathing, the sign the thing inside is alive.
